newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Verplaetse takes over BIS presidency.
newsitem.headline: Verplaetse takes over BIS presidency.

text.p: Compromise and not revolution will be the guiding principle in coming years as the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) continues to adapt to the forces of globalisation, its new president said.

Alfons Verplaetse, governor of Belgium's central bank, on Monday settled in to his job as BIS president, promising to continue the transformation of the world's oldest international financial institution, but still remain true to its origins.

"BIS is developing and I think this development has to go on. But in a balanced way, not completely forgetting its origin, but with its eyes open to the future." Verplaetse, 67, told Reuters in an interview.
Verplaetse, who replaced Wim Duisenberg at the helm of BIS, repeatedly stressed analysis, compromise, pragmatism and an open mind as his guiding principles in moving BIS forward.

"By experience I am a pragmatic bridge builder and think that quality, which my country gave to me -- well, imposed on me -- might be useful for an institution like the BIS which is moving from the past to the future," he said.
Verplaetse will need all his political skills in coming years as BIS comes to grips with European integration and the effect of globalisation on financial markets and stability.
BIS, bank to the worlds' central banks, last year embraced the new economic world order by expanding its membership with nine new central banks from emerging and transition economies.
Verplaetse described this as a first step and only when the impact of this change on BIS has been evaluated -- in about one year -- will the further expansion return to the agenda.

Although he did not exclude further expansion, Verplaetse is concerned that universal membership could jeopardise BIS' role as a focal point for global central bank cooperation, as a club where central bankers huddle in intimate confidentiality.

"In the end you may make the whole world shareholders of BIS and then it would be another International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the role of the BIS as central bank of central banks would be lost," he said.
BIS was founded in 1930 to deal with German War reparations, but its main functions were always as a forum for central bank cooperation and a centre for important financial transactions.
It also provides banking and investment services to more than 100 central banks and is renowned for its expertise in the gold market due to its links with central banks.
"BIS knows better than anybody else what is happening in the gold market," Verplaetse said.
Under Verplaetse the Belgian National Bank has sold 707 tonnes of gold since 1989.

Central bank governors from the Group of 10 (G10) leading countries and other nations gather monthly at BIS' headquarters in this Swiss border city to discuss threats to global monetary and financial stability and find ways to defuse the threats.
"That was its role, that is it role and that will remain its role," Verplaetse said.
Globalisation not only means growing economic importance of emerging markets, but also a blurring of traditional boundaries between banks, securities firms and insurance companies.
Nevertheless, they are still supervised by regulators that are separated by sectoral and national boundaries.
Without the same rules for the same financial products, Verplaetse is concerned about arbitrage, where firms seek to exploit the weakest link in the supervisory chain.
"We not only need better contact to emerging countries, but also to look beyond the frontiers of credit institutions," Verplaetse said.
BIS, the home of the Basle Committee on Banking Supervision, has taken a lead in tackling this challenge and supervisors from the three industries now cooperate in the Joint Forum group.
A major institutional challenge facing Verplaetse is the consequence of several of the European members of G10 joining in a single European Central Bank (ECB).

G10 not only comprises the BIS board, but makes up the core of BIS. The recent expansion of BIS membership was one response to the changes in Europe, but the sensitive issue of whether the new emerging power houses should play a larger role in BIS will be tackled during Verplaetse's watch.
Although a solution must come from Europe, the issue is already weighing on many central bankers.

"It's too early for any conclusion or indication of a possible conclusion. I want to analyse and discuss this with my colleagues and think about it. It's not good to be in too much of a hurry," he said, true to his style.
